units.title: Residual streams, pre-normalization, initialization and residual scaling with depth
outcomes: Explain why a pre-norm block leaves an unnormalized residual stream, and what that does to the stream scale and the last-layer gradient as depth grows.
Derive the variance of the stream after \(N\) independent residual branches and the \(1/\sqrt{N}\) branch scaling that holds it constant.
Compare two initializations by measuring activation and gradient norm growth across layers, and say which claims the measurement cannot support.
units.why: A variant that changes norms, depth or initialization is judged against a baseline whose stream scale already depends on depth. You need the scale argument before you can tell a real architectural effect from a scale effect.

next.note: Move from where the norm sits to what it computes and where it loses precision.
Turn the per-layer scale measurement into a reusable diagnostic.
Ask which initialization rules transfer across width.

study.title: CS336 Assignment 1 handout (Spring 2026 repository)
study.locator: Section 3.3.1 Parameter Initialization (p. 17) and the opening of Section 3.4 (p. 19); then Section 7.3, Ablation 1 and the problem (`pre_norm_ablation`) (pp. 42 to 43)

focus: A pre-norm sublayer reads a normalized copy of the stream but writes into the unnormalized stream. The stream is the embedding plus every earlier branch output, so its scale can grow with depth. A post-norm model renormalizes after every addition. Xiong Lemma 2 states exactly this for their setting: the expected squared norm is flat in depth for Post-LN and grows linearly for Pre-LN.

Theorem 1 bounds one thing: the gradient of the last FFN layer. It is independent of \(L\) for Post-LN and shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{L}\) for Pre-LN. Lemma 3 gives the mechanism: the Jacobian of a normalization scales like \(1/\|x\|\), and \(\|x\|\) is what differs. Read the assumptions before you trust the picture: initialization only, uniform attention (query and key weights zero), one head, square weight matrices and Gaussian inputs.

Two ways to hold the stream scale: scale each residual output projection by \(1/\sqrt{2L}\) (two branches per block), or keep a fixed small standard deviation and rely on normalization. OLMo 2 dropped a depth-dependent scheme for a flat standard deviation of 0.02 and reports growth exponents closer to 0 for activations and gradients. That is one report on its own models with its own measurement, and it compares against OLMo-0424's layer-index scheme, not against uniform \(1/\sqrt{2L}\).

OLMo 2 changed several things as a package (reordered norm, QK-norm, z-loss, initialization). Section 3.3.2 says reordered norm and QK-norm 'in isolation' do not give good results, so the report cannot attribute the gain to any one of them.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the mean square of the stream after \(N\) residual branches whose outputs are independent, zero-mean and each of variance \(v\), on an input of variance \(\sigma_0^2\): \(\sigma_0^2 + Nv\). Scaling each branch by \(1/\sqrt{N}\) gives \(\sigma_0^2 + v\) for every \(N\). Then, on your own pre-norm decoder with random token IDs and no training, record the stream mean square after every block for \(L = 4, 16, 64\), with and without scaling the attention output projection and FFN down projection by \(1/\sqrt{2L}\). Labeled example, not a target: with a toy decoder (width 128, 4 heads, FFN width 344, RMSNorm, normal initialization with variance \(2/(\text{fan-in} + \text{fan-out})\), 4 sequences of 64 random tokens, mean of 3 seeds, PyTorch 2.14.1 on CPU) the final mean square was 2.38, 10.6 and 56.7 for \(L = 4, 16, 64\) unscaled, and 1.14, 1.15 and 1.15 scaled. Growth in the unscaled runs was faster than linear in \(L\) (the increment per sublayer rose from 0.17 to 0.30 to 0.43), so the independence assumption does not hold exactly. Expect the scaled values to stay flat and the unscaled ones to grow.
traps: Reading Theorem 1 as a layer profile. It bounds the last layer only. In the same toy at \(L = 64\) with post-norm, the FFN down-projection gradient norm was 0.160 at the last block and 7.4 at the first, the opposite order to 'gradients are large near the output', while the last-layer value stayed near 0.15 to 0.16 for \(L = 4, 16, 64\) as the theorem says. Pre-norm gave 0.108, 0.049 and 0.022 at the last block. Measure the whole profile in your own model.

Treating the OLMo 2 stability result as evidence for one component. Its Table 1 and Section 3.3.2 describe a package, and Equation 2 in Section 2.1 writes \(\operatorname{MLP}(x)\) where Table 1 and the Section 3.3.2 table use the intermediate state \(h\). Follow the table.

Calling a flat curve of stream norm 'stable'. The stream scale at initialization says nothing about training, and the final norm hides a growing stream from the output head. Compare the stream scale at several points in training before you claim a depth effect.

selfTest.q: Why does a pre-norm model need a final norm before the output head?
selfTest.a: The stream is unnormalized and its scale depends on depth and position in training. Without a final norm the logits would carry that scale. The final norm restores a fixed scale before the head.

selfTest.q: \(N\) branch outputs are independent, zero-mean, each of variance \(v\), and are added to a stream of variance 1. What is the variance after the additions, and after scaling each branch by \(1/\sqrt{N}\)? What changes if the outputs are perfectly correlated?
selfTest.a: \(1 + Nv\), and \(1 + v\) after scaling. If the \(N\) outputs are perfectly correlated, the sum has variance \(N^2 v\), so growth is quadratic in \(N\) and \(1/\sqrt{N}\) scaling no longer holds the scale.

selfTest.q: Why does Theorem 1 give a last-layer gradient that falls like one over the square root of depth for Pre-LN but is flat for Post-LN?
selfTest.a: The Jacobian of the final normalization scales like \(1/\|x\|\). In Pre-LN the squared norm of the stream grows linearly with \(L\), so the gradient shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{L}\). In Post-LN the input to the normalization has a depth-independent norm.

selfTest.q: A colleague says the OLMo 2 report shows depth-scaled initialization is worse than a flat standard deviation. What does the report actually compare?
selfTest.a: A flat standard deviation of 0.02 against OLMo-0424's scheme, which scaled output projections by a factor that depends on the layer index. It measured growth exponents and spike scores in its own setup, alongside other changes. It does not test uniform scaling by one over the square root of twice the layer count.

units.title: RMSNorm, LayerNorm, logit scale and precision hotspots in softmax and normalization
outcomes: Derive RMSNorm from LayerNorm, state when they coincide exactly, and derive the RMSNorm Jacobian \(\frac{1}{r}\left(I - \frac{yy^\top}{d}\right)\).
Derive the z-loss gradient and explain why cross-entropy alone cannot control the logit offset that z-loss controls.
Find the precision hotspots in a block (squares, exponentials, long accumulations) and measure each against a float64 reference at a stated dtype and shape.
Reproduce attention-logit growth in a small model and show what QK-norm does to it.
units.why: Most numerical failures in a decoder sit in three places: the norm, the attention softmax and the output softmax. A variant that changes any of them changes where precision is lost, so you need to know each hotspot before you attribute a loss difference to the mechanism.

next.note: Turn these measurements into dtype and scale tests on your decoder.
See how loss scaling, nonfinite handling and clipping interact with the hotspots found here.

study.title: Small-Scale Proxies for Large-Scale Transformer Training Instabilities (arXiv:2309.14322v2)
study.locator: Section 3.1 (3.1.1 attention logit growth and 3.1.2 output logit divergence), Figures 1 to 4
study.depth: Stop before Section 3.2. The muParam, warmup and depth experiments belong to later units.

focus: LayerNorm is RMSNorm applied to the mean-centred input. The two agree exactly when the feature mean is zero (same \(\epsilon\) and gain, no bias). Add a constant to every feature and LayerNorm does not change, while RMSNorm rescales and keeps the offset. Dropping the mean removes one reduction and the bias parameter, and the claim that this makes the model faster is about memory traffic, not FLOPs.

The Jacobian of a normalization is \(1/r\) times a projection, so gradients through a norm scale like one over the input scale. That is the mechanism behind Xiong's Lemma 3 and behind the learning-rate sensitivity in Wortsman et al.

Softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all logits, so cross-entropy is flat along that direction and nothing stops the offset from drifting. z-loss, \(c(\log Z)^2\) with \(Z = \sum_i e^{z_i}\), adds a gradient \(2c \log Z\) times the softmax along it. QK-norm bounds the attention logits directly: after per-head RMSNorm with unit gains each query and key has norm \(\sqrt{d_h}\), so \(|z| \le \sqrt{d_h}\) before the gains.

Name each hotspot with its failure. Squares in float16 overflow when \(|x| \ge 256\), because \(256^2 = 65536\) exceeds the float16 maximum 65504. bfloat16 keeps the float32 range but has 8 bits of precision, so logits in \([64, 128)\) are rounded to multiples of 0.5. Naive sequential accumulation stalls once the running sum reaches 256 in bfloat16. Library reductions and fused norm kernels accumulate in a wider type, so you must check your own code, not the library's.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the RMSNorm Jacobian at \(\epsilon = 0\) and show that its largest singular value is \(1/r\) with \(r = \sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_i x_i^2}\) and that \(x\) itself is mapped to zero. Show \(\operatorname{LayerNorm}(x) = \operatorname{RMSNorm}(x - \bar{x})\). Then derive the z-loss gradient with respect to the logits, \(\operatorname{softmax}(z) - \text{onehot}(y) + 2c \log Z \cdot \operatorname{softmax}(z)\), and check it against autograd in float64 for \(z = [2, 0, -1]\), \(y = 0\), \(c = 10^{-4}\): the gradient is \([-0.15584, 0.11424, 0.04203]\) with \(\log Z = 2.16985\). Finally, in PyTorch 2.14.1 on CPU, take a float16 vector of 4095 ones and one entry 300. A hand-written `x.pow(2).mean()` gives `inf` and the normalized row is all zeros. After `x.float()` the entries are 0.2086 and 62.59. `torch.nn.functional.rms_norm` on the same float16 input returns finite values because the library upcasts.
traps: Testing a hotspot through the library function instead of your own code. In the check above `torch.nn.functional.rms_norm` is safe in float16, and `torch.ones(10000, dtype=torch.bfloat16).sum()` gives 9984 (a rounded result of a wider accumulation), but a Python loop adding ones in bfloat16 stops at 256. The hand-written norm and reduction in your block are what can fail.

Claiming QK-norm 'fixes' attention logit growth without a baseline run at the same learning rate. Wortsman et al. show growth at high learning rates in small models and relate it to the quadratic dependence of logits on parameter norms; they call that a hypothesis. Run both variants at several learning rates.

Trusting a fused z-loss kernel. OLMo 2 Figure 8 shows a fused implementation and a plain PyTorch one that agree in the forward pass and diverge in the backward pass, and the report suspects precision. Compare gradients, not only the loss value.

selfTest.q: When do LayerNorm (no bias) and RMSNorm give the same output, and what happens to each when you add a constant to every feature?
selfTest.a: They agree when the input already has zero mean over the feature axis, with the same \(\epsilon\) and gain. Adding a constant leaves LayerNorm unchanged, because it subtracts the mean. RMSNorm still divides by the new root mean square, so the constant remains in the output at a different scale.

selfTest.q: Why can't cross-entropy alone stop all the logits from drifting upward together, and what does z-loss add?
selfTest.a: Cross-entropy depends only on logit differences, so adding \(\delta\) to every logit leaves the loss and its gradient unchanged while \(\log Z\) rises by \(\delta\). The term \(c(\log Z)^2\) is not shift-invariant and adds the gradient \(2c \log Z \cdot \operatorname{softmax}(z)\), which pulls \(\log Z\) toward 0.

selfTest.q: After per-head RMSNorm with unit gains, what is the largest possible attention logit \(q \cdot k / \sqrt{d_h}\)?
selfTest.a: \(\sqrt{d_h}\). Each normalized vector has root mean square 1, so norm \(\sqrt{d_h}\), and Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the dot product by \(d_h\). Learned gains multiply the bound, so the observed maximum can exceed \(\sqrt{d_h}\).

selfTest.q: An activation vector in float16 has largest entry 200. Is a hand-written RMS computation safe? What if the entry is 260?
selfTest.a: At 200 the square is 40000, below the float16 maximum 65504, so the square is finite. At 260 the square is 67600, which overflows to `inf`, and every output of that row becomes 0. The threshold is 256 because \(256^2 = 65536 > 65504\).

selfTest.q: Two runs differ only in whether QK-norm is on, and the QK-norm run reaches a lower loss at one learning rate. What else must hold before you credit QK-norm?
selfTest.a: Several seeds at that learning rate, a learning-rate sweep for both variants (the best learning rates may differ), and the same data order and token budget. A single run at one learning rate cannot separate the mechanism from learning-rate sensitivity.

units.title: Gated feed-forward width matching and parameter, activation and KV-memory accounting
outcomes: Derive the gated feed-forward width that matches a two-matrix feed-forward network in parameters, and quantify what rounding the width does to the match.
Derive per-block parameter counts, per-token KV bytes and saved-activation counts for a standard block and for one variant (SwiGLU, GQA), and say which of them a width match leaves unmatched.
Count saved activations in your own block with autograd hooks and reconcile the count with the formula.
units.why: Every later comparison in this section says 'at matched parameters'. A gated feed-forward network matches parameters and matmul FLOPs with its ungated baseline but not activation memory, and a rounded width does not even match parameters exactly. This unit gives you the accounting to state exactly what is matched.

next.note: Apply the same accounting to the attention side: KV bytes for MHA, MQA, GQA and MLA.

study.title: Modern LLM Notebook, Appendix B: From Parameters to Memory
study.locator: Section 1 (Parameters) and Section 2 (Activation Memory)
study.depth: Section 2 lists the tensors a forward pass produces, not the tensors autograd saves, and omits two that a SwiGLU feed-forward network saves. Use it for the layout and recount with hooks. Stop before Section 3.

focus: A gated feed-forward network has three \(d \times h\) matrices and an ungated one has two \(d \times 4d\) matrices, so equal parameters means \(3dh = 8d^2\) and \(h = \tfrac{8}{3}d\). Shazeer's Section 3.1 states the same match as 3072 to 2048 at \(d = 768\): \(2 \cdot 768 \cdot 3072 = 3 \cdot 768 \cdot 2048\).

Real configurations round the width. For \(d = 4096\) the exact width is 10922.67 and OLMo 2 uses 11,008, so the gated block has 0.78% more parameters than a 4x ungated block. State the counted parameters of both variants in any comparison.

Parameters and matmul FLOPs match; saved activations do not. For one token, an ungated GELU feed-forward network at width \(4d\) saves \(2h + d = 9d\) elements for backward (input, pre-activation, activation), while the gated one at width \(\tfrac{8}{3}d\) saves \(4h + d \approx 11.67d\) (input, two projections, the activated gate and the product).

Shazeer's Table 1 reports means with standard deviations of 0.004 to 0.010 for four 65,536-step runs and single values at 524,288 steps. The 0.003 gap between GEGLU (1.633) and SwiGLU (1.636) at the longest run is smaller than that run-to-run spread. The setting is T5 span-filling with Adafactor and no dropout.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, for width \(d = 4096\): derive \(h = 8d/3\), then count a 4x GELU feed-forward network (\(2 \cdot 4096 \cdot 16384 = 134{,}217{,}728\) parameters) against the gated one at width 11,008 (\(3 \cdot 4096 \cdot 11008 = 135{,}266{,}304\)), a difference of 1,048,576 or 0.78%. Then for a block with 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head size 128 and \(d = 4096\), derive 41,943,040 attention parameters (67,108,864 for multi-head) and 4096 bytes of bfloat16 KV cache per token per layer. Finally, wrap each feed-forward module in `torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks`, count unique saved non-weight tensors for \(d = 96\) at widths 384 (GELU) and 256 (SwiGLU), and match \(9d\) and \(11.67d\) elements per token (864 and 1120). The two modules both hold 73,728 parameters. Measured in PyTorch 2.14.1 eager mode, float32.
traps: Calling a width match a cost match. Equal parameters and equal matmul FLOPs leave saved activations and elementwise work different (about 1.3 times the saved elements here), and a recompute or fused-kernel policy changes the saved set again. Report which cost you matched.

Recounting with the notebook's Section 2 recipe. It lists produced tensors, counts a feed-forward block as \(2BSD + 2BSF\) and rounds the gated block's \(6.33BSD\) up to \(8BSD\). Autograd also saves the activated gate and the gated product, and a count from hooks is the check.

Reading the 8/3 rule as exact. Rounding the width to a multiple of 64, 128 or 256 changes the parameter count, and the 4x baseline in the A1 SiLU ablation matches the gated width only 'approximately'.

selfTest.q: Why is the matched gated width \(\tfrac{8}{3}d\) and not \(\tfrac{2}{3} \cdot 4d\) of something else?
selfTest.a: It is the same number: three matrices of \(d \times h\) must equal two matrices of \(d \times 4d\), so \(3h = 8d\). Equivalently the ungated width \(4d\) is reduced by a factor of 2/3.

selfTest.q: A model with width 4096 uses a gated feed-forward width of 11,008. By how many parameters per layer does it differ from a 4x ungated network?
A SwiGLU and a GELU feed-forward network have identical parameter counts. Which one saves more activations for backward, by how much, and why?
selfTest.a: SwiGLU, about 11.67d against 9d elements per token (1.3 times). It saves the shared input, both projections, the activated gate and their product, while GELU saves the input, the pre-activation and the activation.

selfTest.q: Shazeer's Table 1 has GEGLU at 1.633 and SwiGLU at 1.636 after 524,288 steps. What can you conclude about their ranking?
selfTest.a: Nothing firm. The gap is 0.003, the 65,536-step runs have standard deviations of 0.004 and 0.010, and the longest runs are single values. The paper recommends SwiGLU on the whole table, not on that gap.

selfTest.q: Per token and per layer, how many KV-cache bytes does a bfloat16 model with 8 KV heads of size 128 need, and what is the cache for one 8192-token sequence in a 32-layer model?
selfTest.a: \(2 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 4096\) bytes per token per layer. Over 32 layers and 8192 tokens that is \(4096 \cdot 32 \cdot 8192 = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824\) bytes, exactly 1 GiB (1.07 GB).
